title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Oct 20, 2026
intro: Evals and reliability dominate: audit your judges, put SLOs on agent behavior, and test tool interfaces for drift.

cards.title: Audit your LLM judge before trusting its scores
cards.problem: LLM-as-a-judge scores get treated as objective, but the judge model is subjective in its own way.
cards.apply: Treat the judge as a system under test: spot-check its verdicts against human-labeled samples and review disagreements before using its scores to gate releases.
cards.result: Eval regressions you act on reflect real quality changes rather than judge bias.

evidence.note: The source argues LLM judges are subjective; the audit workflow here is the editor's reading, with no measured figure.

cards.title: Give agent behavior an SLO and an error budget
cards.problem: Teams have no shared, quantitative answer to whether an agent is behaving well in production.
cards.apply: Define one or two agent-behavior SLIs (for example task success rate on sampled traces), set an SLO target, and track burn against an error budget as you do for services.
cards.result: Behavior regressions page someone through the same reliability process as outages, instead of surfacing as anecdotes.

evidence.note: Grafana proposes applying SLOs and error budgets to agent behavior; the expected outcome is an editorial inference.

cards.title: Optimize review for minimum human time that doesn't raise reverts
cards.problem: Agents produce code faster than humans can review it, so review becomes the bottleneck.
cards.apply: Raise automated test coverage and add deep automated review first, then shrink human review to the smallest slice that keeps your revert rate flat, using reverts as the guardrail metric.
cards.result: The Claude Code team claims this cuts human review time without raising reverts.

evidence.note: The Claude Code team describes this as the goal they optimized for in their review process.

cards.title: Use small decision models for cheap, fast eval judgments
cards.problem: Frontier-model judges make large eval suites slow and expensive to run on every change.
cards.apply: Route binary eval checks to a purpose-built decision model (such as the recent Decider, d1 or Decisions API class) and keep a frontier judge only for ambiguous cases.
cards.result: Vendors claim these models make evals cheap and fast enough to run per commit; check agreement on your labeled set first.

evidence.note: The source says decision models promise fast, inexpensive judgments; the post's figures are not reproduced here.

cards.title: Test your agent against drifting tool descriptions and schemas
cards.problem: Tool descriptions, argument schemas and tool lists change after deployment while the agent's behavior was only tested on the old text.
cards.apply: Add a regression suite that perturbs tool descriptions, argument names and tool ordering, and fail the build if function-call accuracy drops.
cards.result: Interface changes get caught in CI instead of as silent tool-call failures in production.

evidence.note: The paper studies function calling under interface drift; the CI practice is the editor's application of it.

cards.title: Don't read low injection success as safe in small agents
cards.problem: Low prompt-injection attack success rates can mean a small agent ignored the instruction rather than refused it.
cards.apply: Log whether the agent flagged or refused injected content, not just whether the attack succeeded, and test small models with tasks that still require the injected tool call.
cards.result: Your safety numbers separate real resistance from a model that simply fails to follow instructions.

evidence.note: The paper reports that low attack success rates in small tool-using agents hide ignoring rather than refusing.

cards.title: Keep agent prompts append-only so the KV cache prefix stays reusable
cards.problem: Agents resend the whole conversation each turn, and re-tokenizing it wastes CPU time before the engine can reuse its prefix cache.
cards.apply: Append new turns to an unchanged prefix, never rewrite earlier messages, and tokenize only the new delta when your serving stack allows it.
cards.result: Per-turn latency scales with new tokens instead of full history length.

evidence.note: The paper targets tokenization of session deltas; the practice here is inferred, no figures are claimed.

cards.title: Expose only the relevant skills per step, not the full library
cards.problem: Loading every skill into context grows prompts and makes the agent's choice among skills less reliable.
cards.apply: Index skills by description, retrieve the few relevant to the current step, and inject only those procedures into context.
cards.result: Smaller prompts and fewer wrong-skill selections as the skill library grows.

evidence.note: The paper frames Selective Skill Exposure as necessary for scalable skill use; the expected result is inferred.
